headline: Four years in a Russian prison. Hubbard is coming home.
summary: Russia freed Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday, a 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan held for more than four years on a charge of fighting for Ukraine. The US called his detention wrongful. Trump says he asked Putin by phone last week and gave up no one in return. Five other Americans remain in Russian prisons, their advocates say.

cover_question.q: Why did Russia let him go now?

cover_answer: The Kremlin says mercy. Trump says he asked last week.
table_question: If someone does you a favour, do you owe them one back?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A 74-year-old American teacher named Stephen was kept in a prison in Russia for four years, four birthdays' worth. Today Russia let him go, and he is on his way home to his family. He has been unwell, so doctors will look after him first. The grown-ups worked for a long time to get him home.
5-7.why: Four birthdays and a plane home. Leave the war out unless they bring it.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them four birthdays, a plane and a family waiting. The charge, the war and what his sister says happened to him stay out unless the child brings them. Expect "why was he in prison?" Russia said he fought for Ukraine. America said that was wrong.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Stephen Hubbard, 74, was captured in Ukraine in 2022 after Russia invaded. A Russian court gave him nearly seven years; the US called it wrongful. Last week Trump asked Putin to free him, and on Wednesday Russia did. Releases usually go like trading cards, one for one; this went one for nothing.
8-12.why: Captured, charged, held, freed. The trading card is the mechanism.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect, so the script runs the chain in order: captured, charged, seven years, a phone call, a release. The trading card is the mechanism they know: usually one for one, and not this time. Expect "why give him away for nothing?" The Kremlin says mercy. That week, Trump waived sanctions on Russia.

13-17.script: Is a prisoner release a gift or a receipt? Russia freed Stephen Hubbard with no one traded. The same week Trump waived sanctions on Russia, and says enforcing them would have ended the talks. Second: five Americans are still in Russian prisons. What do their families hear in "welcome home"?
13-17.why: Gift or receipt, then the five still inside.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a man is going home, and the government that freed him got a sanctions waiver the same week, which Trump says saved the talks. The script asks whether that makes the release a gift or a receipt, then adds five families waiting. Expect "so was it a trade?" Not a swap. The rest is argument.

5-7.a: Russia said he fought on Ukraine's side in the war. America said that wasn't right. Now he is free and going home.

8-12.q: Why did Russia let him go?
8-12.a: The Kremlin says mercy. Trump says he asked Putin last week. No trade.

8-12.q: Did he really fight for Ukraine?
8-12.a: A Russian court said so after a closed trial. The US called it wrongful.

13-17.q: Why did Russia let him go now?
13-17.a: The Kremlin says mercy. Trump says he asked, the week he waived sanctions.

13-17.q: What about the other Americans still held?
13-17.a: Five, their advocates say, some seriously ill. Their families ask the same.

caption:
The Kremlin says mercy. Trump says he asked last week.

Russia freed Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday, a 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan held for more than four years on a charge of fighting for Ukraine. The US called his detention wrongful. Trump says he asked Putin by phone last week and gave up no one in return. Five other Americans remain in Russian prisons, their advocates say.

Source: PBS NewsHour
